A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Orak benchmark. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched; reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original gameplay evaluations, arena matches, agent and modality ablations, and fine-tuning generalization results, including Tables 3–7 and game-specific appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds training-data quality/scaling experiments and real-time StarCraft II evaluations in Table 8.

M1.justification: The MCP evaluation pipeline, agent modules, game interfaces, trajectory curation, and supervised fine-tuning procedure are retained. Appendix T discusses possible RL integration, while Sections 4 and U still identify RL fine-tuning as future work; it does not establish a change to the implemented method.

E1.justification: The twelve games, six genres, and Math500/WebShop tasks are retained. Section 5.7 adds continuous real-time StarCraft II evaluation against hard and easy opponents, extending coverage to a scenario where inference latency affects the evolving environment.

E2.justification: Figure 4(b) adds Gemini-2.5-pro matchups and an Elo entry to the StarCraft II arena, expanding the reported comparator set from seven to eight models. This counts despite Gemini already appearing elsewhere. Section 5.3 and Appendix K.5 retain inconsistent seven-model descriptions.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 110K high-score, 110K low-score, and 220K mixed training-data conditions, plus a paused/real-time by hard/easy StarCraft II design. These extend the experimental settings without replacing the existing benchmark splits, metrics, or documented SFT configuration.

E4.justification: Table 8(a) adds a five-game analysis of trajectory quality versus increased training-data volume. Table 8(b) tests sensitivity to inference latency and opponent difficulty. These address substantive questions previously untested, while the existing module, modality, augmentation, and transfer analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 mainly reports means, standard deviations, and trial counts. New Appendix S adds GPT-4o confidence intervals, per-game Welch tests, and cross-game paired tests in Tables 51–53. Appendix C.5 also revises the reported SF3 run count from three-to-five to five; unchanged scores do not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Table 8 adds substantive findings: Darkest Dungeon scores are 92.0 with high-score training versus 40.0 with low-score or mixed data; all three models score zero in hard real-time StarCraft II, while only GPT-4o scores 100 in easy real-time play. Figure 4(b) adds Gemini and revises arena outcomes and Elo values, including Claude from 1550.1 to 1561.4 under the expanded opponent pool. Tables 3–7 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix T adds explicit discounted terminal-score and blended turn-level reward definitions in Equations 2–3, extending v2's qualitative discussion of future RL integration. Existing game-score definitions are retained, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The benchmark, MCP interface, and gameplay dataset contributions remain the same. The introduction softens its visual-input finding from visual states often hindering gameplay to models failing to extract sufficient value from visual inputs, narrowing the asserted negative effect.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning data quality, latency versus accuracy, unsuccessful StarCraft II transfer, and prospective RL integration. Appendix R also newly asserts that a text-only agent performs best in every game, which overstates Table 50: Gemini's combined-input Super Mario score is 40.9 versus 38.0 for the best text-only model.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a direct Hugging Face dataset access link alongside the existing code link. The new studies disclose data-condition sizes and average inference latencies. Existing environment instructions, prompts, preprocessing, SFT hyperparameters, hardware, and training-time documentation are largely retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to FlashAdventure, a system-2 reasoning survey, RAGEN, turn-level RL reward design, and statistical testing references, while removing ST-WebAgentBench. These modestly extend positioning toward reasoning and multi-turn RL; the principal related-work discussion and benchmark comparison remain stable.

P1.justification: There are localized wording edits, an added latency-evaluation subsection, and new Appendices R–T. The previous limitations appendix moves from R to U. An ICLR publication header and additional affiliation appear, but most prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 4(b) expands its heatmap and rating table to eight models and relabels the rating column as Elo. Table 8 adds two experimental panels; Table 50 primarily consolidates existing results, and Tables 51–53 display new statistical analyses. Other figures and table designs are largely retained, with renumbering and layout reflow.

improvement.justification: Table 8 addresses previously untested data-quality and real-time applicability questions, and the dataset link improves access information. However, Figure 4(b) ranks Gemini's 1512.3 above GPT-4o's 1525.0, and Table 52(a) labels its comparator as Llama-3.2-3B although several statistics match the 1B baseline, including SF3 t=4.644. These inconsistencies undermine the expanded comparative evidence, leaving the net quality effect uncertain.
